title: Showing numbers on fingers
keyIdea: You can show a number on your fingers: one finger up for each one. To check, touch each finger that is up once and say a number for it; the last number you say tells how many. One hand has 5 fingers, so for 6 to 10 you show a full hand of 5 and some more on the other hand. The same number can be shown in different ways: 3 fingers and 2 fingers make 5, and so do 4 and 1.

kid: Hold up one finger. That is 1. Put up one more. That is 2. Each finger up is one more.
Touch each finger that is up. Say a number for each one: 1, 2, 3. Stop at the last one. The last number is how many.
One hand has 5 fingers. Want to show 7? Put up all 5 on one hand. Then 2 more on the other hand: 6, 7.
Put up 3 on this hand and 2 on that hand. That is 5! You can make 5 lots of ways.
adult: Showing numbers on fingers is part of early number in the EYFS. Development Matters asks three and four year olds to show 'finger numbers' up to 5 and to link numerals and amounts, and US Common Core K.CC.B.4 and K.CC.B.5 ask children to count to tell how many and to know that the last number said is the total. Finger patterns also build subitising: seeing a small amount without counting.

The key ideas are one-to-one correspondence (one number word for each finger), the cardinal principle (the last number said tells how many) and the part-whole structure of numbers. Showing 7 as a full hand and 2 more uses 5 as an anchor, which NCETM's Mastering Number programme calls '5 and a bit'. Showing 5 as 3 and 2 or 4 and 1 is early work on the composition of 5.

Common mistakes: putting up the right fingers but not checking, counting one finger twice or skipping one, thinking the first number said is the total, always holding up a whole hand, and trying to show 6 or more on one hand. A common adult slip is insisting on one 'correct' set of fingers; any fingers will do if the amount is right, and showing a number in more than one way is worth praising.

In the lab your child taps fingers up and down to show 3, 2 and 4, touches each finger that is up to count it, shows 7 and 9 with a full hand and some more, makes 5 three different ways on two hands, and puts a finger down each time one of five little ducks swims away.

familyTip: Ask finger questions in everyday moments: "How old are you? Show me." "Show me 3 for the 3 grapes." Then count the fingers together, touching each one. Sing 'Five Little Ducks' and put one finger down each time a duck swims away.

visual.caption: How many fingers? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: show numbers on fingers, touch each finger to count, use 5 and some more, make 5 three ways, sing five little ducks.

practice.prompt: How many fingers are on one hand?
practice.hint: Hold up one hand and touch each finger as you count.
practice.explain: One hand has 5 fingers, counting the thumb. Two hands have 10.

practice.prompt: You hold up {n} fingers. You put 1 finger down. How many fingers are up now?
practice.hint: One finger down is one less.
practice.explain: {n} fingers, then one goes down, leaves {=n-1} fingers up.

practice.prompt: Kit wants to show 6 on her fingers. What can she do?
choices: 5 on one hand and 1 on the other
practice.hint: How many fingers are on one hand? Is that enough for 6?
practice.explain: One hand only has 5 fingers. A full hand of 5 and 1 more on the other hand makes 6.

practice.prompt: One hand shows all 5 fingers. The other hand shows {k}. How many fingers are up?
practice.hint: Start at 5 and count on the other hand: 6, 7…
practice.explain: 5 and {k} more make {=5+k}. Say 5, then count on for each finger on the other hand.

pool.prompt: Ben holds up {n} fingers. He touches each one and counts. What is the last number he says?
pool.hint: One number for each finger that is up.
pool.explain: He says one number for each of his {n} fingers, so the last number is {n}. That is how many.

pool.prompt: Ana counts her fingers from the thumb. Ben counts the same fingers from the little finger. What happens?
pool.hint: Do the fingers change when you start at the other end?
pool.explain: The fingers stay the same, so the count is the same. You can start counting anywhere.

pool.prompt: {a} fingers up on one hand and {b} on the other hand. How many fingers are up?
pool.hint: Count the fingers on both hands.
pool.explain: {a} and {b} more make {=a+b}. Count them all to check.

pool.prompt: Ana is 3 years old. Which shows how old she is?
pool.explain: 3 years, so 3 fingers up. Count them: 1, 2, 3.

pool.prompt: Five little ducks are on the pond. One swims away. How many fingers do you hold up now?
pool.hint: One duck went, so one finger goes down.
pool.explain: 5 ducks, then one swims away, leaves 4 ducks. So 4 fingers stay up.

pool.prompt: You hold up all 10 fingers. You put {k} down. How many fingers are still up?
pool.hint: Put the fingers down one at a time and count what is left.
pool.explain: 10 fingers with {k} down leaves {=10-k} still up.

pool.hint: Count the fingers on both hands.
pool.explain: 3 and 2 make 5. 3 and 3 make 6, and 4 and 2 make 6 too.

pool.prompt: Ben has 3 fingers up. He counts 1, 2, 3, 4. What went wrong?
pool.hint: He said more numbers than there are fingers.
pool.explain: He has 3 fingers, so he should say 3 numbers. Saying 4 means one finger got counted twice.
